630: An altercation is a heated, noisy, and angry argument between two or more people. It is a verbal clash — a moment where people are loudly disagreeing, often with raised voices, sharp words, and visible emotion. Think of it as an argument that has gone past the point of calm discussion and crossed into openly hostile, aggressive exchange.
The qualities that define an altercation

Not every disagreement is an altercation. Three qualities are almost always present:

It is heated. The people involved are emotionally charged — angry, frustrated, or confrontational. There is nothing mild or polite about it.

It is noisy. An altercation is not a quiet, private disagreement. It is the kind of argument that other people around can hear and notice.

It is openly hostile. The tone is aggressive. People in an altercation are not trying to reason with each other calmly — they are clashing.
Is it physical or just verbal?

This is an important and slightly nuanced point. An altercation is a verbal event — it is about angry words, not fists. However, in real-world usage (especially in news reports and police or legal language), the word is sometimes used for incidents where the heated argument also involved minor physical contact, like pushing or shoving. It would not typically be used to describe a full-on fistfight or a violent assault — those would be called a "brawl," a "fight," or an "assault."

So think of it this way: an altercation lives in the space between a heated argument and a physical fight. It is always angry and confrontational, always verbal, and may sometimes spill into minor physical aggression — but it is not a beating or a battle.
Where it sits among similar words

Understanding a word well means knowing how it differs from its neighbors.

An argument is a broad, neutral word. It can be calm, logical, and quiet. An altercation cannot — it is always heated and disruptive.

A dispute is even broader and more formal. Two countries can have a territorial dispute that plays out in diplomatic meetings over years. An altercation is always immediate, personal, and emotionally charged.

A quarrel is the closest everyday synonym. The difference is subtle — a quarrel can be more private and low-key, even between friends or family. An altercation tends to suggest more intensity, more noise, and often a more public or serious setting.

A squabble is a petty, minor bicker over something trivial. An altercation carries more weight and seriousness.

A brawl is a physical fight. An altercation is not.
The register: when and where is this word used?

Altercation is a formal word. You would typically see or hear it in news articles, police reports, legal documents, and formal writing — not in casual conversation. If you say to your friend, "I had an altercation with my brother over the remote control," it would sound oddly formal and even a little comical, because the word carries a gravity that doesn't fit a trivial sibling squabble.

But if a news article reads, "Police were called after an altercation broke out between two men outside the nightclub," that sounds perfectly natural — because the context is serious, public, and formal.

A heated altercation broke out in the parking lot after the two drivers accused each other of cutting in line.

The meeting ended abruptly when a brief altercation between two board members forced the chairman to intervene.

Witnesses reported that the altercation began over a noise complaint and quickly grew loud enough to disturb the entire neighborhood.

Despite the altercation earlier in the day, both parties agreed to return to the negotiating table.

An altercation is a loud, angry, and heated verbal clash between people — more intense than a regular argument, more serious than a squabble, less physical than a fight — and is a formal word typically found in news, legal, or official contexts.
631:
Alterity means otherness — the quality or state of being "the other," of being fundamentally different from a point of reference, which is usually a self, a group, or a dominant perspective. Whenever someone or something is experienced as "not me," "not us," or "not the same," the quality of being "the other" is what alterity refers to.

It is almost synonymous with the word "otherness," but alterity is the more precise, technical, philosophical term you'll encounter in academic writing, cultural theory, and theology. The two words can often be used interchangeably, but alterity carries more philosophical weight.
The essential dynamic: self and other

Alterity only makes sense as a relationship. It always involves two sides: a self (also called "the same") and an other. The self defines itself partly by what it is not — and what it is not is "the other." Alterity is the quality that belongs to that other side.

Think of it this way: you know who you are partly because you know what you are not. You are not your neighbor. You are not a person from a completely different culture. The quality of "not-being-you" that your neighbor has, from your perspective, is their alterity. It is the irreducible gap between the self and everything outside of it.

This is not merely about surface-level differences like hair color or taste in music. Alterity points to something deeper — the experience of encountering someone or something that is fundamentally outside your own frame of reference and cannot be fully absorbed, reduced, or explained away by you.
Radical alterity: the deepest form of the concept

The most important and philosophically rich idea tied to alterity is what thinkers call radical alterity — the idea that the "other" is not just different from you in passing or trivial ways, but is irreducibly, permanently, and fundamentally other. No matter how deeply you try to understand another person, you cannot fully enter their inner experience. There is always something about them that remains beyond your reach. That unbridgeable gap — that sense that the other can never be fully contained by your understanding — is radical alterity.

The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas built much of his ethical philosophy around this idea. He argued that when you encounter the face of another person, you are confronted with their radical alterity — their absolute otherness. That other person cannot be reduced to your ideas about them, your categories, your memories, or your experiences. They are, in a sense, infinite: they always exceed what you think you know about them. And this irreducible otherness, Levinas said, is the very foundation of ethical responsibility. Because the other person is not just a version of yourself — because they are genuinely, radically other — you are obligated to take their existence seriously, to recognize them, to be responsible for them. Ethics, in his view, begins not with abstract rules, but with the encounter with this otherness.

Alterity is also one of the most important concepts in thinking about how societies, nations, and groups relate to one another — especially across lines of race, culture, gender, and power.

When a dominant group labels another group as "alien," "foreign," "strange," or fundamentally incomprehensible, they are assigning alterity to that group — constructing them as the radical "other." This is how many forms of prejudice, racism, and colonialism have historically worked: a powerful group defines itself as "the norm" or "the default" and projects alterity onto those it marginalizes. The "othered" group is portrayed as fundamentally different, exotic, threatening, or unknowable.

The scholar Edward Said analyzed exactly this in his landmark work on "Orientalism" — the way Western cultures constructed Eastern cultures as their radical other, defining them as mysterious and alien, as a way of affirming a Western identity and justifying colonial domination. The "Orient" was not described on its own terms; it was constructed as the alterity of the "Occident" (the West).

This points to one of the most important tensions in the concept: alterity can be experienced and used in two very opposite ways.

On one hand, genuinely recognizing another person's alterity — acknowledging that they are irreducibly other, that you cannot fully know them or reduce them to your categories — can be the foundation of deep respect, humility, and ethical responsibility.

On the other hand, assigning alterity to a group — labeling them as so fundamentally "other" that they are incomprehensible or threatening — has historically been used as a tool of oppression, dehumanization, and exclusion.

The difference lies in whether you respond to the other's otherness with respect and openness, or with fear and the desire to dominate.
How alterity compares to similar words

Difference is the most general word — any two things can be different in any number of ways. Alterity is more specific: it implies a particular kind of difference, the difference between a self and what it encounters as other, often carrying a sense of irreducibility and depth.

Otherness is nearly synonymous and can often be substituted for alterity. The practical distinction is that alterity is the formal, technical term preferred in philosophy and academic writing, while otherness is more common in everyday speech.

Diversity focuses on the variety and coexistence of many differences within a group or society. Alterity focuses on the relational quality of being "the other" to a specific self or perspective — it is about the encounter between two sides, not the variety within a whole.

Foreignness and strangeness are narrower, more everyday words that suggest surface-level unfamiliarity. Alterity is broader and more philosophical — it can apply to any encounter with an other, whether that is another person, another culture, another idea, a work of art, or even, in theology, God.

In personal life: When you try deeply to understand someone who has lived a completely different life — a different country, language, history, trauma, or joy — and realize that no matter how carefully you listen, you cannot fully enter their inner experience, you are encountering their alterity. They remain irreducibly other, and that gap deserves acknowledgment and respect.

In history and politics: When colonial powers described indigenous peoples as "savages" or as fundamentally incomprehensible, they were constructing those peoples' alterity — fabricating a radical "otherness" to justify conquest and domination.

In philosophy (Levinas): The alterity of the other person — their absolute otherness — is what makes ethics possible and necessary. If the other were just a version of you, you could absorb them into your own understanding. It is precisely because they are not you, because they are irreducibly other, that you owe them recognition and care.

In theology: In many religious traditions, God's alterity refers to God's radical transcendence — God is so fundamentally "other" from human beings that no human concept or category can fully contain or capture God. God is not just a bigger or better version of a human; God is alterity itself.

In literature and art: A reader or viewer may encounter the alterity of a fictional world, a narrator, or a character — the ways in which a text confronts you with something genuinely outside your own experience, forcing you to step outside yourself and inhabit a perspective that is fundamentally other.

Once you understand alterity, you begin to see the question it raises everywhere:

Can I truly understand someone whose inner life is fundamentally different from mine? How should I treat someone whose otherness I cannot reduce or eliminate? How do societies use the idea of "the other" to define themselves — and who gets harmed by that process? What does genuine respect for another person actually require?

At the heart of alterity is a profound and humbling idea: the other person — and by extension, every genuinely different culture, perspective, or being — always exceeds your ability to fully know them. They are never simply a reflection or extension of you. They remain, at some level, irreducibly other.

Recognizing that can be uncomfortable, because it means accepting a permanent gap in your understanding. But many thinkers argue it is also the beginning of genuine wisdom: the willingness to sit with that gap, to not paper it over with stereotypes or assumptions, and to let the otherness of the other make a real claim on you — ethically, intellectually, and humanly.
632:
When something alternates, it switches back and forth between two things repeatedly, in a pattern. Think of a see-saw: one side goes up, then the other, then the first again, then the other again — neither side stays up permanently. That steady, recurring back-and-forth is exactly what "alternate" captures.

Three things define the word: it almost always involves two options (not a random jumble of many), the switching repeats over and over (it isn't a one-time change), and neither side is permanent.

When two things naturally take turns with each other, you say they alternate, or that one alternates with the other.

"Day and night alternate." / "Rainy seasons alternate with dry ones."

Here, both things are equal participants — both taking turns, neither one controlling the other.

When one thing switches between two states, you say it alternates between them.

"She alternated between excitement and nervousness before the show." / "The weather alternated between freezing and mild all week."

Here, a single subject is the one doing the shifting — back and forth between two conditions it finds itself in.

When a person actively switches between two things, they simply alternate those things.

"The coach alternated the two players throughout the match." / "She alternated chocolate and vanilla layers in the cake."

Here, a person is deliberately in control of the back-and-forth — they're choosing to keep switching.

Repetition is everything. Switching from coffee to tea once and staying there is just changing. But switching from coffee to tea, then back to coffee, then back to tea, over and over — that is alternating. The pattern must keep going. A single switch is never enough.

It usually involves two defined things. You alternate between hot and cold, work and rest, speaking and listening. The word is built for a clear pair. You wouldn't normally say someone "alternated among" ten random, unrelated things.

The regularity can be loose. A traffic light alternates between red and green with perfect, precise timing. But a person can alternate between being confident and being anxious without following any exact schedule. The word only requires a noticeable pattern — not a mathematical one.

Nature: The seasons alternate year after year, moving from warmth to cold and back to warmth.

Design: The artist painted the fence posts in an alternating pattern — red, white, red, white, all the way down.

Sports: The two teams alternate possession of the ball.

Music: The song alternates between a quiet, delicate verse and a loud, crashing chorus.

Emotion: During the long wait for his results, he alternated between hope and dread.

Work schedule: She alternated between working from the office and working from home each week.

Exercise: The trainer had him alternate between sprinting and walking to build stamina.

It doesn't mean simply "change" or "switch." A permanent change is not alternating. If a city used to have cold winters but now has warm winters permanently, its climate hasn't "alternated" — it has changed. Alternating always implies the back-and-forth keeps repeating.

It also doesn't mean doing things randomly or chaotically. The word carries a sense of structure — a recognizable, deliberate or natural rhythm of back-and-forth.
To alternate = to go back and forth between two things, repeatedly and in a pattern, with each side taking its turn.
633:
"Alternately" means in turns — two things keep switching back and forth, one after the other, in a repeating pattern.

The pattern it describes looks like this:

A → B → A → B → A → B → ...

Two things. Taking turns. Over and over.

Picture a seesaw. One side goes up, then down, then up, then down — endlessly switching between two positions. That rhythm of back-and-forth is exactly what "alternately" captures.

Or picture traffic lights that flash red, then green, then red, then green. Two states, switching in turns.

"She alternately laughed and cried during the film."
→ She laughed, then cried, then laughed, then cried — her emotions kept going back and forth between these two states.

"The doctor said to alternately apply hot and cold packs."
→ Hot pack first, then cold pack, then hot again, then cold again. The two temperatures switch in turns.

"He was alternately kind and cruel to his students."
→ At times kind, then cruel, then kind again — two behaviours, flip-flopping repeatedly.

"The coastal road alternately hugs the clifftops and dips down to the beach."
→ The road goes up near the cliffs, then down to the beach, then up again, then down — back and forth between two positions.

"The sky was alternately bright and overcast all afternoon."
→ The sun came out, then clouds rolled in, then sun again, then clouds again.

Notice the pattern in every example: two things, switching in turns, more than once.
What Types of Things Can "Alternately" Describe?

Almost anything can alternate — emotions, actions, physical states, colours, sounds, conditions, places. As long as two things are switching back and forth, "alternately" fits.

  • Emotions: She was alternately nervous and excited.
  • Colours: The tiles were alternately black and white.
  • Sounds: The alarm alternately beeped and buzzed.
  • Behaviors: He alternately paced the room and sat down.

This is where most learners go wrong, and getting this right will set you apart.

These two words look nearly identical but mean completely different things.

"Alternately" = two things switching back and forth in turns (a pattern of behaviour)

"Alternatively" = a different option is available (a choice between two things)

WRONG: "You can take the train. Alternately, you could fly."

RIGHT: "You can take the train. Alternatively, you could fly."

Here, you are offering a choice — fly instead of taking the train. There is no back-and-forth pattern. You pick one or the other. So the correct word is "alternatively."

RIGHT: "During the match, he alternately sprinted and jogged to manage his energy."

Here, he kept doing both — sprinting, then jogging, then sprinting, then jogging. It's a back-and-forth pattern. So "alternately" is correct.

The quick test: Ask yourself: "Am I describing something that keeps switching back and forth between two things?" → Use alternately. "Am I presenting a second option or choice?" → Use alternatively.

• It does not mean "sometimes" or "occasionally." ("He alternately felt sad" is wrong if he just felt sad now and then. There must be two things switching back and forth — sad and something else, in turns.)
  • It does not mean "on the other hand" or "as a second option." That's "alternatively."
  • It does not mean randomly switching. There's a sense of sequence and pattern — not chaos.
  • It does not describe one thing happening once. The back-and-forth must happen at least a couple of times to justify using "alternately."

"Alternately" usually sits just before the two verbs or adjectives it connects:

  • "She alternately smiled and frowned." (before the verbs)
  • "The wall was alternately painted red and white." (before the adjectives)

Less commonly, it can open a sentence describing a pattern:

  • "Alternately, the machine heats and cools the metal."

But avoid using it at the start of a sentence to introduce a second option — that's the job of "alternatively."

"Alternately" describes a back-and-forth pattern between two things, where each one takes its turn, over and over:

A → B → A → B → A → B

Always two things. Always switching. Always sequential.

Its most dangerous look-alike is "alternatively," which means "as another choice" — a completely different job. Keep these two straight, and you have full command of the word.
634:
When "alternative" is used as an adjective, it describes something that is not the main, standard, or usual thing — but a different option that could be used instead.

Think of it this way: whenever you have a primary or default thing, and then you have something else that could replace or substitute for it, that something else is "alternative."

The word always carries the silent idea of choice and substitution — you could use this instead of the usual one.

In everyday use, "alternative" most commonly means "serving as a different option you can choose in place of the main one."

Examples:

  • "The highway is blocked. Let's take an alternative route." — Not the usual road, but a different road you could take instead.
  • "Do you have an alternative plan if this doesn't work?" — A backup plan, different from the current one.
  • "We need an alternative source of water." — Not the usual/main source, but a different one that can serve the same purpose.

In all these cases, notice that "alternative" signals: this is not the first or default choice, but it exists as a replacement.

The word does not suggest the alternative is better or worse. It simply says: here is another option available to you.
Sense 2: Outside the Mainstream or Conventional

"Alternative" has a second, more specific shade of meaning — and this one is important. When used in certain phrases, it means "consciously departing from what is conventional, mainstream, or widely accepted."

It's not just another option here. It's specifically one that stands apart from or challenges the dominant, established way of doing things.

Examples:

  • Alternative medicine — Medical approaches (like herbal treatments, acupuncture, or homeopathy) that exist outside of conventional/mainstream Western medicine. They offer a fundamentally different philosophy about healing.
  • Alternative energy — Energy from non-conventional sources like solar, wind, or geothermal, as opposed to traditional fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas).
  • Alternative music — A style of music that rejects or avoids the conventions of mainstream commercial pop music.
  • Alternative lifestyle — A way of living that differs significantly from widely accepted social norms.
  • Alternative education — Teaching methods and philosophies that are different from the standard school system.

In these phrases, "alternative" carries a cultural weight — it quietly implies: this is not what most people do or accept as the norm, and it is deliberately different.
A Key Nuance: There Is Always an Implied Comparison

Whenever "alternative" is used as an adjective, it always implies the existence of a primary or standard thing, even if that thing isn't named.

When someone says "an alternative approach," they are implicitly saying: "There is a standard/usual approach, and this is NOT that — this is a different one."

You cannot use "alternative" without this implied reference point. The word's entire meaning depends on the idea that something more standard exists, and this is a departure from it.

It helps to understand how "alternative" differs from words that seem similar:

  • "Different" just says two things are not the same. "A different route" simply means another road — no implication of substitution. "An alternative route" specifically means a road you could use instead of the usual one.
  • "Other" is even more neutral. "Another plan" just means one more plan exists. "An alternative plan" means a plan ready to replace the main one if needed.
  • "Substitute" is close in meaning, but is used more as a noun or verb, and it focuses on the act of replacing something. "Alternative" is softer — it just makes itself available for replacement; it doesn't necessarily claim to be a substitute for something that has failed.

So "alternative" is more specific than "different" or "other" — it always carries the idea of a genuine choice between this and something else.

Traditionally (and you may still see this in formal writing), "alternative" was used only when there were exactly two options — because choosing one meant you couldn't choose the other. For example: "The two alternatives were to fight or retreat."

In modern, everyday English, however, this strict rule has largely been abandoned. People now use "alternative" for any number of options, not just two. So phrases like "there are several alternative solutions" are completely normal and accepted today.

Here are patterns you'll frequently encounter:

  • an alternative + noun → an alternative solution, an alternative path, an alternative source
    (= a different option you could use instead)
  • alternative + noun (as a compound/set phrase) → alternative medicine, alternative energy, alternative music, alternative lifestyle
    (= something outside the mainstream)
  • alternative to → "This is an alternative to surgery."
    (= this can replace/substitute for surgery)

As an adjective, "alternative" describes something that:

  1. Is not the standard, main, or default option — but exists as a different possibility.
  2. Represents a genuine choice — you could pick this instead of the usual thing.
  3. Sometimes (especially in fixed phrases) means outside the cultural or professional mainstream — deliberately different from what is widely accepted.

The word always quietly points to a "standard thing" in the background and says: "This is a different path from that one, and you could take it."
635:
An alternative is one of the possible options you can choose from when you are in a situation where a decision must be made.

The word always implies that there are at least two possibilities in front of you, and that picking one means you are not picking the other. The options stand in place of each other — they compete for your choice.

Think of it this way: you are at a fork in the road. Each path you could take is an alternative. You can only walk down one.

A few things make this word special, compared to simply saying "option" or "choice":

1. There is always a context of decision. You do not use the word "alternative" in a vacuum. It only makes sense when someone is weighing what to do. There is always an implied question: "What do we do?" or "Which way do we go?" The alternatives are the answers being considered.

2. The options are mutually exclusive. This is the most important characteristic. If you choose one alternative, you are giving up the others. You cannot take all the alternatives at once. They are substitutes for each other, not additions to each other. For example, if your alternatives are to quit your job or to ask for a raise, doing one rules out the other (at least as a response to the same situation).

3. It often carries the sense of "instead of something else." An alternative is frequently presented as a substitute for something that is usual, expected, or already being considered. When a doctor says "surgery is one alternative," they mean it is one possible path instead of the other paths (medication, rest, etc.). There is always a sense of replacement or substitution baked into the word.
How many alternatives can there be?

Strictly in traditional usage, "alternative" was used only when there were exactly two choices (because the word has roots tied to the idea of "the other one of two"). Even today, careful writers and speakers sometimes prefer to use it only for two-way choices.

However, in everyday modern English — and this is completely accepted — people use "alternative" for any number of choices: two, three, five, ten. You will regularly hear:

"The committee reviewed five alternatives before making a decision."

So, as a learner, you can safely use "alternative" whether there are two choices or many. Just know that its strongest, clearest use is in a two-way choice — and that some careful speakers might raise an eyebrow if you use it loosely for a long list of options.

One of the most common and meaningful uses of this noun is in the phrase "there is no alternative" or "I had no alternative."

This does not literally mean zero options existed. It means: there was effectively only one sensible or possible course of action, so there was no real choice to be made. The person felt forced, not free.

For example:

"I had no alternative but to fire him — he had stolen from the company."

This means: the situation left only one acceptable path. Any other path was either impossible or unacceptable.

This usage is very common and very natural. Understanding it is important because it shows you that "alternative" is deeply tied to the freedom to choose — when that freedom disappears, there is "no alternative."

Everyday life:

"We missed the last train. Our alternatives were to take a taxi or stay at a hotel."

Two paths stood before them, and they had to pick one.

Work and business:

"The budget was cut, so the team explored alternatives to hiring a full-time designer."

They were looking for substitute solutions instead of the usual approach.

Medicine:

"The surgeon explained that there were three alternatives: immediate surgery, a wait-and-watch approach, or medication."

Three mutually exclusive paths were on the table.

Everyday with "no alternative":

"With the bridge washed out, we had no alternative but to turn back."

Only one path was possible.

These three words overlap a lot, but here are the useful distinctions:

  • Choice is the most general word. It refers to any act of selecting, or anything that can be selected. It has no special implication of substitution or competition between options.
  • Option is also fairly general, but it leans slightly toward the idea of something available to you — a door that is open, a possibility you can take up or leave. It is flexible and neutral.
  • Alternative is more specific. It carries the clearest sense that the options are in competition with each other, that selecting one replaces the need for the others, and that there is a real decision to be made. It also often (though not always) carries a slight sense that it is something different from what is standard or usual — a substitute, a workaround, another way.

In casual speech, people use these three words interchangeably, and that is fine. But when you want to emphasize the idea of "instead of something else" or "mutually exclusive paths," "alternative" is your most precise and powerful choice.

An alternative is one of two or more mutually exclusive options available in a situation where a decision must be made, with the core idea being that choosing it means giving up the others — and it often implies something that stands in place of what is usual or already being considered.
636:
Altitude means the height of something measured above a fixed reference point. That reference point is almost always sea level — the average surface level of the world's oceans.

So when you say something has a high altitude, you are saying it sits far above the ocean's surface level, even if there is no ocean anywhere nearby.
The Key Idea: Why a Reference Point Matters

Height is always measured from something. If you say a bird is flying "20 meters high," the listener asks: high from where? The ground? A rooftop? That's vague.

Altitude solves this problem by fixing a single, universal starting point: sea level = zero. Everything is measured upward from there. This makes altitude a precise, universally comparable measurement. A mountain in Nepal and a mountain in Peru can be meaningfully compared because both are measured from the same baseline.
Altitude in Everyday Life and Geography

This is the most common use. When people say a city, mountain, lake, or village is "at a certain altitude," they mean how high that place sits above sea level.

  • Mount Everest has an altitude of about 8,849 metres. That means its peak is 8,849 metres above sea level.
  • Mexico City has an altitude of about 2,240 metres, which is why visitors sometimes feel breathless when they first arrive — the air up there is thinner.
  • A coastal city like Mumbai has an altitude close to zero, because it sits right at the ocean's edge.

Pilots use the word "altitude" constantly. When an aircraft is in flight, its altitude is how high it is above the ground or above sea level at any given moment.

  • "The aircraft is cruising at an altitude of 10,000 metres."
  • Pilots must always know their altitude to avoid mountains, other aircraft, and to land safely.

In aviation, altitude can be measured in two slightly different ways:

  • Above sea level (ASL): The standard and most widely used reference, consistent everywhere.
  • Above ground level (AGL): How high the aircraft is above the actual ground directly below it. This matters during takeoff and landing. An aircraft could be 3,000 metres above sea level but only 50 metres above a tall plateau it is about to land on.

Both are valid uses of the word altitude, and context tells you which one is meant.

In astronomy, altitude takes on a slightly different but related meaning. It refers to how high a star, planet, or any celestial object appears in the sky above the horizon, measured as an angle in degrees.

  • If a star is sitting right on the horizon (barely visible), its altitude is 0 degrees.
  • If a star is exactly overhead (directly above your head), its altitude is 90 degrees.
  • Any star in between has an altitude somewhere from 0° to 90°.

So in this context, altitude is not a distance in metres but an angular measurement. The underlying idea, however, is the same: how high something is above a fixed baseline (the horizon instead of sea level).

In geometry, altitude has a precise, technical meaning. The altitude of a shape — most commonly a triangle — is an imaginary straight line drawn perpendicularly (at a perfect 90° angle) from one side of the shape to the opposite corner (called a vertex).

Think of a triangle sitting on its flat base. The altitude is the straight vertical drop from the top corner down to the base, meeting the base at a right angle. It is essentially the "height" of the triangle, used in calculating its area.

  • For a triangle, Area = ½ × base × altitude.

Every triangle has three altitudes (one from each vertex to the opposite side). In geometry, it's important to distinguish altitude from a side of the shape — the altitude is not necessarily a side; it is a measured height.
Altitude vs. Elevation — What's the Difference?

These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, and that is perfectly fine. Both refer to height above sea level.

However, there is a subtle technical distinction:

  • Elevation is typically used for fixed points on the Earth's surface — cities, mountain peaks, roads, lakes.
  • Altitude is more commonly used for things above the surface and in motion — aircraft, rockets, birds — or in scientific and aviation contexts.

In practice, you will often see both used for mountains and geographical features without anyone objecting. "The elevation of Everest" and "the altitude of Everest" are both correct and widely accepted. But you would say a plane's altitude, not its elevation.
The Real-World Effects of High Altitude

Understanding altitude is not just academic — it has real physical consequences.

Air pressure and oxygen: The higher you go, the lower the air pressure, and the less oxygen there is in each breath. At sea level, your lungs work easily. At 5,000 metres, the air has roughly half the oxygen density of sea level. At the top of Everest (~8,849 m), it has about one-third.

Temperature: Altitude generally causes temperature to drop. As you climb higher, the air gets colder — roughly 6.5°C cooler for every 1,000 metres of altitude gained. This is why mountain peaks are snowy even in tropical countries.

Altitude sickness: When people who are not acclimatised (not used to altitude) go too high too fast, they may experience headaches, nausea, dizziness, and shortness of breath. This is called altitude sickness (also known as acute mountain sickness or AMS). It happens because the body struggles to get enough oxygen from the thin air. Gradual ascent, rest, and sometimes supplemental oxygen are used to manage it.

Boiling point of water: At higher altitudes, water boils at a lower temperature than 100°C (its sea-level boiling point) because of lower air pressure. At very high altitudes, food cooked in boiling water takes longer to cook for this reason.

• "The Tibetan Plateau has an average altitude of over 4,500 metres, making it the highest plateau on Earth."
  • "The pilot announced that we had reached our cruising altitude of 11,000 metres."
  • "Astronomers noted that Saturn was at an altitude of 45 degrees above the horizon last night."
  • "To find the area of this triangle, you need to measure its base and its altitude."
  • "Trekkers are advised to rest for a day when they reach an altitude above 3,500 metres to let their bodies adjust."

Altitude is always about height above a reference baseline. In geography and daily life, that baseline is sea level. In aviation, it is either sea level or the ground below. In astronomy, it is the horizon. In geometry, it is the base of a shape. The word is consistent in spirit — how high is this thing above the line we've agreed to start measuring from? — even as the specific reference point shifts depending on the field.
637:
Altruism is the genuine care for the well-being of others, acted upon without seeking any personal reward. When someone demonstrates altruism, their driving force is simply this: I want this other person (or creature) to be better off. Not because they expect something back. Not to look good. Just because they care.

It is one of the most powerful ideas in human life — the idea that a person can act entirely for someone else's sake.
The one thing that makes it altruism

The single defining feature of altruism is selfless motivation. The action must come from a genuine desire to benefit someone else, not yourself.

Consider two scenarios. In the first, you help a colleague finish a project because you know they'll return the favor someday. In the second, you help them simply because you see they're overwhelmed and you want to ease their burden — and you ask for nothing in return. Only the second is altruism. The action might look identical from the outside, but the why is everything.
What altruism is NOT

This is where many people get confused, so it's worth being precise.

Altruism is not the same as being generally nice or friendly. Everyday politeness — holding a door, saying thank you — doesn't rise to the level of altruism. Altruism involves a conscious, active concern for another's welfare, not just social habit.

Altruism is not helping someone to gain a reward. If you donate to a charity so people admire you, or help a neighbor expecting them to owe you one, that is transactional behavior — an exchange. True altruism has no hidden invoice.

Altruism is not helping out of guilt. If you're moved purely by the discomfort of not helping — to relieve your own guilty conscience — then your primary concern was actually about yourself, not the other person.

Altruism is not pity. Pity is looking down at someone from a distance. Altruism is a genuine concern for their well-being, which puts you and them on equal footing.
"But what if helping others makes me feel good?"

This is one of the most common and interesting questions about altruism, and you deserve a clear answer.

Many people experience what researchers call a "helper's high" — a genuine feeling of warmth or satisfaction after helping someone. This does not cancel out altruism, and here's why: what matters is your primary intention. If you helped someone because you genuinely wanted to improve their situation, and you felt good afterward as a side effect, that's still altruism. Feeling good was the consequence, not the goal.

It only stops being altruism if the emotional reward was the entire reason you acted — if, deep down, you helped someone not for their sake but purely to chase that good feeling for yourself.

This distinction is the subject of one of philosophy's oldest debates. Some thinkers — called psychological egoists — argue that truly selfless motivation is impossible, because humans always get something out of every action (even if it's just emotional satisfaction). Others argue this is too cynical and stretches the idea of "self-interest" beyond all usefulness. In everyday language, and in most serious discussions, altruism simply means that your dominant, primary concern was the other person's well-being — not your own.
Altruism in real life

To make this concrete, here are genuine examples of altruism:

A bystander who jumps into a river to save a drowning stranger, risking their own life, with no time to calculate reward. A person who anonymously donates a large sum of money to a hospital in another country they'll never visit. Someone who regularly gives blood, not for recognition, but because they know it saves lives. A person who gives up their seat on a packed train to someone who needs it more, without waiting for a "thank you."

Notice that these range from small and simple to large and dramatic. Altruism is not always heroic — it lives in small, quiet moments just as much as in extraordinary ones.
Altruism in philosophy and ethics

In moral philosophy, altruism is generally treated as a virtue — a genuinely good quality of character. It sits at the opposite end of the moral spectrum from selfishness.

The philosopher Auguste Comte, who coined the word in the 19th century, believed altruism was the foundation of a moral society — that humans ought to live for others, not just themselves. Later, philosopher Peter Singer pushed this idea further, arguing that if we can prevent something bad from happening to someone else at little cost to ourselves, we are morally obligated to do it.

Many ethical traditions — from utilitarianism (which values actions by how much good they produce for all people) to religious ethics — place altruism at or near the center of moral life.
Altruism in psychology

Psychologists classify altruism as a type of prosocial behavior — any action that benefits others. What makes altruism specifically interesting to researchers is that it often involves a cost to the person helping: their time, their money, their energy, sometimes even their safety.

Studies have found that altruism is a real, consistent, measurable tendency in humans — not just an ideal. People regularly help strangers, donate organs to people they've never met, and devote their lives to causes that benefit no one in their personal circle. Psychologists have found that factors like empathy, a sense of social responsibility, and even mood can increase altruistic behavior.
Altruism in biology

The concept even appears in nature, where it is called biological altruism. Worker bees, for example, will sting a predator to protect the hive, even though the act kills them. Meerkats take turns standing guard to warn the group of danger, exposing themselves to risk so others can feed safely.

Biologists debate whether animals have genuine motivations (the way humans do), but the behavior itself fits the pattern: one organism reducing its own advantage to benefit others. Evolutionary biologists have developed theories — like kin selection (helping relatives who share your genes) and reciprocal altruism (helping others who may help you in the future) — to explain why such behaviors evolved. However, it's worth knowing that these biological mechanisms are slightly different from the full philosophical meaning of altruism, which requires conscious intention.
Effective Altruism — a modern movement

In recent decades, a global movement called Effective Altruism has brought the concept into sharp, practical focus. Its core idea is this: if you genuinely want to help others, you should try to help them as much as possible with the resources you have.

Rather than donating to a charity because it feels meaningful to you personally, an effective altruist asks: which cause actually saves the most lives, or reduces the most suffering, per dollar? They treat helping others not just as a good impulse, but as a serious project to be done rigorously and thoughtfully. It's altruism made deliberate, rational, and evidence-driven.
Degrees of altruism

Altruism isn't a single, fixed thing — it exists on a spectrum. At one end, helping a close family member could be seen as partly self-serving, since their happiness directly affects yours. Helping a friend is a step further. Helping a stranger is further still. Helping someone you'll never know, in a part of the world you'll never visit, at real cost to yourself, is considered the most "pure" form.

The further removed the other person is from your personal world, and the greater the sacrifice required of you, the more unambiguous and powerful the altruism.
The opposite of altruism

The direct opposite is egoism or selfishness — acting purely for your own benefit, with no genuine concern for the effect on others. Altruism and egoism represent two ends of a spectrum of human motivation, and most real-world behavior lands somewhere between them.
Related word forms

Altruist (noun) refers to a person who practices or embodies altruism: "She's a genuine altruist — she's spent thirty years quietly helping people with no interest in recognition."

Altruistic (adjective) describes an action or person characterized by altruism: "It was a deeply altruistic decision to donate his inheritance to strangers."
The simplest summary

If you want to carry just one sentence with you: Altruism is doing something good for someone else, purely because you want them to be better off, with nothing in it for yourself. Everything else — the philosophical debates, the biological examples, the modern movements — is an expansion of that one central idea.
638:
When you describe someone or something as altruistic, you mean that it is focused on the well-being of other people, with no expectation of personal gain or reward in return.

An altruistic act is one where the sole motivation is to benefit someone else — not to look good, not to feel good afterward, not to earn a favour back, and not to gain anything material. The "someone else" matters more than "yourself" in that moment.
The One Thing That Makes It Truly Altruistic

The defining ingredient is selflessness. If there is a hidden personal benefit — even a subtle one — the act starts to lose its "altruistic" label.

Think of it like a sliding scale. On one end, you have a completely selfish act (done purely for yourself). On the other end, you have a completely altruistic act (done purely for others). Most human behaviour sits somewhere in the middle, which is why the word "altruistic" carries real weight when it is used — it signals that someone has leaned very far toward the "others" end of that scale.

A wealthy person who donates a large sum of money to a charity anonymously — meaning no one knows they gave it, so they get no praise, no recognition, no tax receipt, no public applause — is behaving altruistically. There is nothing in it for them. The only outcome is that someone else's life improves.

A stranger who jumps into a river to save a drowning child, at serious risk to their own life, without stopping to think about it, is acting altruistically. Their instinct is entirely about the other person's survival, not their own.

A doctor who travels to a war zone or a poverty-stricken region, giving up a comfortable, well-paying career to treat patients who cannot pay, is described as altruistic.

Contrast this with someone who volunteers at a charity, but mainly because it looks good on a job application. That act has an altruistic surface but a self-serving core — so it would not be accurately described as truly altruistic.

Understanding what a word does not mean sharpens your understanding of what it does mean.

Altruistic is the opposite of selfish or self-serving. A selfish person prioritises their own interests above others'. An altruistic person does the reverse.

It is also different from simply being kind or nice. Kindness can be habitual, social, or even strategic. Altruism specifically involves a conscious or instinctive sacrifice of personal benefit for someone else's sake. You can be kind while also getting something back. You cannot be truly altruistic while also getting something back.

It is different from reciprocity (doing something nice because you expect something nice in return) and from obligation (helping a friend move house because you feel you owe them one). Both of those have a personal motivation attached.

In real-world usage, "altruistic" does not always demand absolute purity. People use it to describe behaviour that is predominantly selfless, even if there might be a small side benefit to the person acting.

For example, scientists who dedicate their lives to researching cures for diseases that don't affect them personally are often called altruistic, even though they may also enjoy the intellectual challenge of their work. The word is being used to signal that their primary, overriding motivation is the benefit of others — and that is enough for the label to apply.

So in everyday speech, altruistic means the dominant motivation is the benefit of others, not necessarily that there is absolutely zero personal gain whatsoever.

There is a long-standing and genuinely interesting debate among philosophers and scientists about whether truly altruistic acts are even possible.

The argument goes like this: when you help someone, you often feel good afterward. That good feeling is a reward — a personal benefit. So were you really acting for them, or were you also acting to get that warm feeling? If helping others makes you happy, is your helpfulness really selfless?

This debate does not make the word useless. It simply means that when philosophers use "altruistic," they use it very strictly. When ordinary people or journalists use it, they use it more loosely to mean someone who genuinely prioritises others' well-being over their own comfort or interests, without expecting a visible reward.

Knowing this distinction will help you understand the word at a deeper level, no matter what context you encounter it in.
How It Is Used in Context

Altruistic is commonly used to describe people, actions, motives, and organisations.

You might describe a person as altruistic ("She is one of the most altruistic people I know"), an act ("That was a genuinely altruistic gesture"), a motive ("His reasons were entirely altruistic"), or even an institution ("The foundation operates on altruistic principles").

It is frequently used in discussions of charity, medicine, philosophy, psychology, evolutionary biology (scientists debate whether altruism exists in animals), and public policy.

Since you are learning the word in its adjective form, it helps to know the family it belongs to:

The noun is altruism — the quality, value, or principle of caring for others above oneself. ("Altruism is rare in competitive environments.")

The adverb is altruistically — in a manner that is altruistic. ("She acted altruistically, refusing any payment.")

The noun for a person is altruist — someone who consistently behaves altruistically. ("He was known as a true altruist.")

If you had to carry just one sentence in your head, let it be this:

Altruistic means acting to benefit others, with no expectation of personal reward — where the well-being of others is the goal, not a means to your own gain.

Everything else in this explanation is simply the detail that surrounds and strengthens that core idea.
639: Alumnus means a person who has studied at and graduated from a particular school, college, or university. If you went to Harvard and finished your degree there, you are a Harvard alumnus. The word is simply a formal, widely respected way of saying "a former student of a place."
It is not just one word — it is a family of four words

This is the most important thing to understand about "alumnus," because the word changes its form depending on the gender of the person and whether you are talking about one person or many. These four forms are all nouns, and they all carry the same core meaning.

Alumnus refers to a single male graduate. "He is an alumnus of Oxford."

Alumna refers to a single female graduate. "She is an alumna of Oxford."

Alumni is the plural form used when referring to a group of male graduates, or a mixed group of male and female graduates together. "The alumni of this university are very accomplished."

Alumnae is the plural form used when referring to a group made up entirely of female graduates. "The alumnae of the all-women's college gathered for a reunion."

Think of it this way: if you are ever talking about a single person, you use either alumnus (for a man) or alumna (for a woman). If you are talking about multiple people, you use either alumni (for a mixed or all-male group) or alumnae (for an all-female group).
The most common mistake people make

Many people mistakenly say "She is an alumni" or "He is an alumni." This is incorrect, because alumni is a plural word and cannot refer to just one person. To talk about a single person, you must always use the singular form — either alumnus or alumna.

While the word is most commonly used for graduates of academic institutions, it has expanded in modern usage to cover former members of any structured organisation or program — a company, a training program, a fellowship, or even a sports team. For example, a person who used to work at Google might be casually called a Google alumnus. The key idea always remains the same: this is someone who was once part of something, completed their time there, and has since moved on.

Language evolves, and so has the use of this word. In modern everyday English, many people and organisations now use alumni as a gender-neutral plural for any group of graduates, regardless of gender — and this is widely accepted. Some also use alumnus as a gender-neutral singular, though this is less universally agreed upon. If you want to be entirely safe and traditional, stick to the four-form system described above. If you want to be modern and inclusive, using alumni as a general plural for any mixed group is perfectly acceptable today.

Imagine a university that has thousands of former students. The institution as a whole refers to all of them as its alumni. Among those thousands, one woman, Dr. Sarah Chen, is a distinguished alumna. One man, Mr. James Ford, is a celebrated alumnus. And a group consisting only of women from the class of 1995 would be referred to as alumnae.

The word carries a sense of pride and belonging. To call someone an alumnus or alumna of a place is to acknowledge that they were formally part of that institution, that they completed something meaningful there, and that they carry a connection to it for the rest of their lives. This is why universities spend so much effort building alumni networks — communities of former students who remain connected to the institution and to each other long after graduation.
